correctness.rationale: For v>b each orientation velocity has fixed sign and magnitude at least ε. Over each finite trajectory segment the occupation time of a spatial null set is zero, so any invariant probability has absolutely continuous spatial components. Its integrable total flux is constant and therefore zero. The common orientation flux solves the scalar linear stationary equation with slope L on force +b segments and −R on force −b segments; continuity of flux through the cusps leaves one normalization and proves uniqueness. The normalized solution satisfies the stationary transport equations; both tails are integrable exactly for L,R>0, equivalent to the stated strict bias inequality. With A=1/L+1/R the right and left masses are proportional to Ae^(aL)−1/L and Ae^(aR)−1/R. In the critical window their ratio is logistic up to exponentially small end corrections and a(L−R)=θ(1+ε/(2b+ε)); Taylor expansion gives the stated first correction uniformly on compact θ-sets. For α±→r the rescaled exponents εL,εR both tend to r; translated well densities converge in L¹ by exponential domination while the inner truncations recede, giving total variation and independence. If dimensionless bias diverges while α±→r, both tail exponents still grow and the sign of a(L−R) gives the claimed polarized limit. On each regular segment f=−b·sgn(Yε), so zero flux makes the orientation mismatching Yε have conditional probability ε/(2v) exactly. No claim at v=b is needed. value.rationale: The vanishing opposing speed makes the order of the symmetry and active-threshold limits consequential. The result identifies the scale of directional bias that still leaves both wells populated, gives each well's asymptotic weight plus its first correction, and resolves the width and shape of the peaks in the same limit. This sharp classification is useful beyond just recomputing a stationary density, without making claims about kinetics or thermal smoothing.
